lessons.title: The Myth of More Information
lessons.key_idea: The naive belief that more information automatically leads to truth and wisdom is wrong, and history shows why.

lessons.title: Information Connects More Than It Informs
lessons.key_idea: Information's main job is to link people into networks, so a story can be powerful without being true.

lessons.title: Stories and Documents Build Societies
lessons.key_idea: Shared stories and bureaucratic records let huge numbers of strangers cooperate, creating realities like nations and money.

lessons.title: The Dream of an Infallible Source
lessons.key_idea: Attempts to bypass human error with holy books or perfect authorities fail, because someone must always interpret them.

lessons.title: Self-Correction Is What Saves Us
lessons.key_idea: Networks that can admit and fix their own mistakes, like science, outperform those that cannot, like the systems behind the witch hunts.

lessons.title: Democracy and Dictatorship as Networks
lessons.key_idea: Democracies spread information through many independent channels while dictatorships centralize it, and this shapes how each handles errors.

lessons.title: AI: A New Member of the Network
lessons.key_idea: AI is an agent that makes its own decisions, so our survival depends on building strong self-correcting institutions around it.

plan.title: Nexus
plan.author: Yuval Noah Harari
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's central arguments, structure and main examples well, though I would avoid quoting fine details or exact figures.
plan.one_liner: More information hasn't made us wiser. Here's why, and what AI changes about it.
plan.summary: Harari asks why humans, after collecting so much information, still act so unwisely. He argues that information is mainly a way to connect people, not a way to represent the truth. Stories, holy books and bureaucratic documents let millions of strangers cooperate, but they can bind people around fictions and delusions just as easily as around facts. What separates healthy networks from dangerous ones is whether they have strong self-correcting mechanisms, such as independent courts, a free press and scientific institutions. He reads democracies and dictatorships as two different kinds of information network. He then argues that AI is something new. It is not just a tool but an agent that can make decisions and create ideas on its own. That forces us to build institutions able to catch and fix its mistakes before they spread.
